domain_label: Plated-Jewelry Quality Grading, Durability Acceptance Tests & Cost-Quality Value Engineering
purpose: A method for grading plated fashion-jewelry quality against a citeable durability acceptance battery (thickness/label class, adhesion, tarnish/salt-spray/porosity, wear/abrasion, nickel release) and then value-engineering a lower price without lowering that graded quality by moving the base-metal, plating-thickness, barrier-layer, finish and batch-economics levers while holding the acceptance gate constant, never crossing a quality gate to save cost and never hardening a screen-grade result into a claimable [FACT].
assumptions: the durability test standards are cited published facts (FTC Jewelry Guides 16 CFR Part 23 thickness/label ladder [FACT]; ASTM B571 adhesion battery [FACT]; ISO 9227 / ASTM B117 salt spray [FACT]; ASTM D4060 Taber abrasion [FACT]; EN 1811 nickel release 0.5 ug/cm2/week prolonged contact, 0.2 for piercing posts, with EN 12472 wear-and-corrosion pre-conditioning [FACT]; ferroxyl / ASTM B735 porosity [FACT]); no market prices, unit-sales counts or brand claims are invented

'high-quality' is multi-dimensional and gate-based, not a single number: a piece is high-quality only if it passes every acceptance test that its label class and wear duty require, at the worst-case point, not on average

the cost-vs-quality relationship is a diminishing-returns curve, not linear: below a floor the piece fails a gate and is worthless; above a knee, extra gold micron and testing buy little added real durability and mostly perceived quality [ESTIMATE, method-level]

value engineering means holding the acceptance gate fixed and moving a lever (base metal, thickness placement, barrier/underlayer, finish system, batch/run economics) to cut cost; a cost-down that fails to re-pass the same battery is a quality cut, not value engineering [METHOD]

in-house screens (ferroxyl, wrap-bend, artificial sweat, rub jig, color panel) control process drift cheaply but are NOT claimable; accredited send-out results (EN 1811 nickel release, conformant salt-spray, certified karat/thickness) anchor any legal or marketing claim [FACT on the in-house/accredited split]
every non-fact is tagged [ESTIMATE] (with method+confidence), [METHOD] (a way to measure), or [UNKNOWN]; screen-grade results are never quoted as accredited [FACT]
exclusions: the substrate/base-metal properties themselves (kb1_substrates_base_metals owns brass/925/316L/zinc mechanical and nickel-release science; this KB accepts them as inputs to the value-engineering levers)

the finish chemistry and rhodium/gold science in depth (kb2_finishes_rhodium_gold owns the micron/thickness classes, barrier-strike and tarnish/anti-oxidation mechanism; this KB uses them as graded levers)

the retail pricing, keystone markup, contribution margin and CAC/LTV verdict (the economics specialist owns turning a cost-engineered COGS into a price; this KB stops at the graded, cost-engineered spec)
market demand, solid-vs-plated share, demographic purchase rates and brand mapping (the market specialist owns those as measurement methods, never invented here)
actual accredited test execution and lab-accreditation advice for a specific filing; this models the grading-and-value-engineering decision procedure, not a live lab report

competency_questions.question: What does 'high-quality' mean for a plated fashion-jewelry piece, and how is it graded rather than asserted?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: QUALITY_DEF_GRADING states quality is multi-dimensional and gate-based (thickness/label class, adhesion, tarnish/corrosion, wear, nickel-safety, appearance), graded at the worst-case point against a citeable battery, not a single number

competency_questions.question: Which thickness classes and measurements gate the label and the durability claim?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: THICKNESS_CLASS_LADDER states the FTC ladder (flash/wash <0.175um, gold electroplate >=0.175um of >=10k, heavy gold electroplate >=2.5um, vermeil = sterling base + >=2.5um gold) and XRF/coulometric measurement at the worst-case point as [FACT]

competency_questions.question: How is adhesion tested and how is cohesive cracking distinguished from an adhesive-failure reject?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: ADHESION_TEST states the ASTM B571 battery (wrap/bend, cross-hatch tape, heat-quench) and the rule that hard-gold hairline cracks with no lifting are cohesive (not a reject) while flakes/peel exposing underlayer are adhesive failure (reject)

competency_questions.question: How are tarnish and corrosion resistance tested, and why do rhodium/barrier layers raise the grade?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: TARNISH_CORROSION_TEST states salt spray (ISO 9227 / ASTM B117) and artificial-sweat screens, the silver-tarnish vs rhodium/barrier mechanism, and that in-house fog boxes are comparative-only while accredited chambers anchor claims

competency_questions.question: How is wear/abrasion durability tested and graded against wear-through to the underlayer?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: WEAR_ABRASION_TEST states Taber (ASTM D4060) / reciprocating-rub / pencil-hardness screens, deposit hardness (soft ~60-90 HV vs hard Co/Ni gold ~130-200 HV), and acceptance = no base-metal/underlayer exposure at agreed cycles vs a retained standard

competency_questions.question: How is nickel safety tested and what limit gates skin-contact legality?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: NICKEL_RELEASE_TEST states the DMG spot test as a screen and EN 1811 (0.5 ug/cm2/week prolonged contact, 0.2 for piercing posts) with EN 12472 wear pre-conditioning as the accredited pass/fail gate under REACH

competency_questions.question: How is porosity tested and why is it the decisive failure mode over an active base metal?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: POROSITY_TEST states ferroxyl (Fe-indicator, ideal for steel/iron cores) and ASTM B735 nitric-vapor methods, the galvanic small-anode/large-cathode pore cell where the noble coating accelerates base-metal corrosion, and that porosity falls steeply above ~1-2.5um noble metal

competency_questions.question: Which acceptance tests gate the 'high-quality' claim, and how is the acceptance plan structured?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: ACCEPTANCE_TEST_PLAN states the pre-production qualification (witness coupons, worst-case specimens, three-conforming-lots, written numeric criteria, AQL/ISO 2859 sampling) and per-batch routine, and GRADE_GATE_MAP maps which tests must pass to earn a high-quality/label claim

competency_questions.question: What is the cost-vs-quality tradeoff curve, where are its floor and diminishing-returns knee, and what drives cost?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: COST_DRIVERS enumerates the quality cost drivers (gold/rhodium micron consumption, Ni/Pd underlayer, hardener, labor/QC time, send-out test amortization) and COST_QUALITY_CURVE states the below-floor-worthless / above-knee-diminishing-returns shape as a [METHOD] curve

competency_questions.question: Which value-engineering levers lower price without lowering graded quality?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: VE_BASE_METAL, VE_THICKNESS_TUNING, VE_BARRIER_LAYERS, VE_FINISH_SELECTION and VE_BATCH_ECONOMICS each state a concrete cost-down lever and the gate it must still pass, including the classic barrier/underlayer lever that cuts gold micron while raising durability

competency_questions.question: How do you avoid false economies that cross a quality gate or trade real durability for perceived quality?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: FALSE_ECONOMY_TRAP names the gate-crossing cost-downs (too-thin flash on active base metal, deleted Ni underlayer, nickel non-compliance) and PERCEIVED_VS_REAL_QUALITY separates visible finish/weight/packaging from real durability that must still pass the gate

competency_questions.question: What is the value-engineering decision procedure, and what graded, cost-engineered spec does it hand off?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: VE_DECISION_PROTOCOL states hold-the-gate / move-one-lever / re-run-the-same-battery / accept-only-if-it-passes, HONESTY_LEDGER separates [FACT] anchors from screen-grade [ESTIMATE]/[UNKNOWN], and VE_HANDOFF delivers the graded cost-engineered spec to the economics/assortment layers

glossary.definition: For plated fashion jewelry, quality is not a single number but a pass across a battery of acceptance gates sized to the piece's label class and wear duty: thickness/label class, adhesion, tarnish/corrosion, wear/abrasion, nickel-safety and appearance, each judged at the worst-case point (recess, inside of ring, high-wear edge), not on average. A piece is 'high-quality' only when it clears every gate its claim requires.

The US FTC Jewelry Guides class structure [FACT]: 'gold flashed/washed' < 0.175 um; 'gold electroplate' >= 0.175 um of >=10k fineness gold; 'heavy gold electroplate' >= 2.5 um; 'vermeil' = a sterling-silver base + >= 2.5 um gold (a base-metal-core piece can never be vermeil, whatever the thickness). Every marketing word on the label is therefore a measured thickness/fineness number, verified by XRF (ISO 3497 / ASTM B568) or coulometric (ISO 2177 / ASTM B504).

The qualitative adhesion practice family [FACT]: 180-degree wrap/bend over a mandrel, cross-hatch + pressure-sensitive tape pull, and heat-then-quench. Pass = no flaking/lifting at magnification; the key discipline is distinguishing cohesive hairline cracking of hard gold at a tight bend (expected, not a reject) from adhesive peel/flake exposing the underlayer (a reject that triggers a prep-chain audit).

Neutral salt-spray accelerated corrosion: 5% NaCl fog at 35 C for a duration ladder (commonly 24/48/96 h for decorative classes) [FACT]. Chamber conformity (temperature, fallout rate, pH) is what makes hours claimable; a DIY fog box is a comparative in-house screen only, and an accredited chamber anchors any printed corrosion claim.

The EU skin-contact compliance test [FACT]: EN 1811 measures released nickel with a 0.5 ug/cm2/week limit for articles in prolonged skin contact and 0.2 for piercing posts, after EN 12472 wear-and-corrosion pre-conditioning that simulates worn plating exposing a nickel underlayer. A dimethylglyoxime (DMG) spot test is a cheap qualitative screen; only the accredited EN 1811 result is a legal document.

Through-pores in a thin noble coating over an active base metal create a small-anode/large-cathode galvanic cell in which the noble gold/rhodium cathode accelerates corrosion of the exposed base metal at the pore [FACT: mechanism]. Detected cheaply by the ferroxyl test (Prussian-blue spots at iron pores, ideal for steel cores) or ASTM B735 nitric-vapor; porosity falls steeply above ~1-2.5 um of noble metal, so a thin flash that looks perfect can be a corrosion time-bomb.

The diminishing-returns relationship between spend (gold/rhodium micron, underlayer, hardener, QC/testing) and graded durability [METHOD/ESTIMATE]: below a floor the piece fails a gate and is worthless regardless of appearance; through the working band each added micron/test buys real durability; above a knee, extra spend buys mostly perceived quality and little added gate margin. Value engineering targets the knee, not the floor.

glossary.term: value engineering (lower price, same graded quality)
glossary.definition: The discipline of cutting unit cost by moving a lever (base-metal choice, plating-thickness placement, barrier/underlayer architecture, finish system, batch/run economics) while holding the acceptance gate constant and re-passing the same battery [METHOD]. A cost-down that changes what the piece can pass is a quality cut, not value engineering; a genuine VE move (e.g. a hard Ni underlayer letting a thinner gold survive wear) can lower cost and raise durability at once.

The written, numeric pass/fail criteria set BEFORE testing (thickness class, pore count, bend class, wear cycles, nickel limit, color tolerance) that a piece must clear to earn its label and 'high-quality' claim. Criteria invented after seeing results always pass; the gate is only real if written first and tested on worst-case witness coupons that rode with the production lot.

Perceived quality is what a buyer senses without a lab (color/shade, gloss, heft, finish uniformity, packaging); real quality is what the acceptance battery measures (adhesion, thickness at wear points, porosity, corrosion, nickel-safety). Value engineering may cut cost on invisible over-spec above the knee without touching perceived quality, but must never cut real quality below a gate to preserve a perceived-quality illusion.

nodes.definition: Establish what 'high-quality' means for a plated fashion-jewelry piece so it is graded, not asserted. Quality is multi-dimensional and gate-based: a piece must clear each of thickness/label class, adhesion, tarnish/corrosion resistance, wear/abrasion, nickel-safety, and appearance, sized to its label claim and wear duty [FACT: the dimensions map 1:1 to published test families]. Every gate is judged at the worst-case point (recess, inside of a ring, a high-wear edge), never on the proud average, because that is where a plated piece actually fails in service. This node fixes the vocabulary the whole KB grades against and rejects any single-number 'quality score' as unsupportable [METHOD].

excluded: the individual test methods (the test nodes)
the cost of achieving each gate (COST_DRIVERS)

pros.claim: Defining quality as a gate-set makes 'high-quality' testable and defensible instead of a marketing adjective
pros.example: a ring earns 'high-quality' only by clearing thickness+adhesion+wear+porosity+nickel at its inside-band worst point, not by looking shiny in a photo

cons.claim: A multi-gate definition is heavier than a single grade and can feel bureaucratic at tiny scale
cons.example: a hobby maker may resist running five test families per product before the first sale

failure_modes: collapsing quality to one dimension (e.g. gold micron) and shipping a piece that fails porosity or nickel
grading on the proud average surface where the plating is thickest instead of the worst-case point
acceptance_tests: the six quality dimensions, the worst-case-point rule, and the label-claim/wear-duty sizing are stated, with single-number 'quality scores' rejected
revisit_triggers: a new product category adds a wear duty (e.g. a ring vs an earring) that resizes the gates
a regulation adds a dimension (e.g. a new substance limit)
a customer-return pattern reveals an ungated failure mode

base.update_signal: a new category, regulation, or return-pattern changes the gate-set

nodes.definition: Fix the thickness gate that governs both the label's legality and the piece's wear life. The US FTC Jewelry Guides (16 CFR Part 23) ladder [FACT]: 'gold flashed/washed' < 0.175 um; 'gold electroplate' >= 0.175 um of >=10k fineness gold; 'heavy gold electroplate' >= 2.5 um; 'vermeil' = sterling-silver base + >= 2.5 um gold (a base-metal-core piece is never vermeil at any thickness [FACT]). Thickness is measured non-destructively by XRF (ISO 3497 / ASTM B568) and cross-checked destructively on a witness by coulometric anodic dissolution (ISO 2177 / ASTM B504), always at the worst-case low-current-density point, since recesses can be at half the average thickness. Every marketing word on the label is therefore an XRF acceptance number, and XRF calibrated on the wrong stack reads garbage [FACT: practice].

included: XRF and coulometric measurement at the worst-case point
excluded: the finish chemistry that deposits the gold (kb2)
the cost of the micron (COST_DRIVERS)

pros.claim: Tying every label word to a measured thickness class makes the label legally defensible and the wear life predictable
pros.example: calling a piece 'heavy gold electroplate' only after XRF confirms >=2.5 um at the inside band prevents a mislabel and a fast wear-through

cons.claim: Worst-case-point XRF on curved/small parts is fiddly and needs correct-stack calibration foils and small-spot collimation
cons.example: a thin-wire piece needs a flat ride-along coupon because curvature degrades the XRF reading

failure_modes: labeling a base-metal-core piece 'vermeil' (reserved for a sterling base)
quoting the proud-surface average thickness while the wear point is at half the class minimum
acceptance_tests: the FTC flash/GEP/HGE/vermeil thresholds, worst-case-point XRF+coulometric measurement, and the never-vermeil-on-base-metal rule are stated
revisit_triggers: the FTC guides or a market's marking law is revised
a new base metal changes the XRF calibration stack
a label word (e.g. 'heavy gold electroplate') is added to a product claim

base.update_signal: a marking-law, calibration-stack, or label-claim change occurs

nodes.definition: Define the adhesion gate: does the coating stay bonded through forming and wear. The ASTM B571 practice family [FACT] runs a 180-degree wrap/bend over an own-diameter mandrel, a cross-hatch grid + pressure-sensitive tape pull, and a heat-then-water-quench that exposes interfacial weakness the tape misses. Pass = no flaking or lifting at 4x-10x. The load-bearing discipline is failure-mode discrimination: hard (Co/Ni-alloyed) gold micro-cracks at a tight bend with NO lifting = cohesive, expected, not an adhesion reject; lifted flakes or peel exposing the nickel/base metal = adhesive failure = reject the lot and audit the pre-clean/strike chain [FACT]. Tape alone is the weakest probe and never a release basis.

excluded: the wear behaviour after adhesion passes (WEAR_ABRASION_TEST)
the strike/underlayer chemistry that drives adhesion (kb2)

pros.claim: A layered battery plus failure-mode discrimination catches real delamination while not rejecting harmless cohesive cracking
pros.example: 10x inspection separates a hard-gold hairline crack (accept) from a flake exposing nickel (reject and audit prep)

cons.claim: Discrimination needs magnification and judgement, and heat-quench temperatures are substrate-specific handbook ranges [ESTIMATE]
cons.example: an operator without a loupe can misread a cohesive crack as an adhesion failure and scrap a good lot

failure_modes: releasing on a passing tape test alone while a wrap/heat-quench would have exposed peel
rejecting a lot for cohesive hard-gold cracking that is expected and not an adhesion defect
acceptance_tests: the B571 wrap/tape/heat-quench battery and the cohesive-vs-adhesive discrimination rule are stated, with tape-alone flagged insufficient
revisit_triggers: a new base metal or strike layer changes the adhesion chain
a forming step (bending a ring) is added that stresses adhesion
a batch shows peel exposing the underlayer

base.update_signal: a base-metal, strike, or forming change stresses adhesion

nodes.definition: Define the corrosion/tarnish gate that sets service life. Screens: neutral salt spray (ISO 9227 / ASTM B117, 5% NaCl at 35 C, 24/48/96 h ladder) [FACT] and artificial-sweat soak (NaCl + lactic acid + urea, pH ~4.5-6.5, 30-40 C, 24-96 h) [FACT: structure]; sulfur-vapor/humidity tests for tarnish. Acceptance = no red rust or base-metal corrosion product, and no visible tarnish/color shift, at the agreed hours. The mechanism the grade rewards: silver tarnishes because it reacts with trace sulfur to form dark Ag2S, while a hard, bright, tarnish-resistant rhodium (a platinum-group metal) or e-coat topcoat is a barrier that keeps the surface bright [FACT]. In-house fog boxes are comparative screens only; conformant-chamber (T, fallout, pH controlled) or accredited results anchor any printed corrosion/'tarnish-resistant' claim [FACT].

included: the silver-tarnish vs rhodium/topcoat barrier mechanism
excluded: porosity as the pore-cell pathway (POROSITY_TEST)
the rhodium/gold deposition chemistry (kb2)

pros.claim: Grading corrosion against a standard chamber ties a 'tarnish-resistant' claim to evidence instead of hope
pros.example: 96 h NSS with no base-metal corrosion product substantiates a service-life claim a DIY fog box cannot

cons.claim: Conformant/accredited corrosion testing is slow and send-out, so it cannot gate every batch
cons.example: salt-spray hours for a label claim take weeks of lab lead time, unlike the daily color-panel screen

failure_modes: quoting salt-spray hours from a non-conformant DIY fog box as if claimable
making a 'tarnish-free' claim with no substantiation test behind it
acceptance_tests: the salt-spray and artificial-sweat screens, the silver-tarnish/rhodium-barrier mechanism, and the in-house-vs-accredited split are stated
revisit_triggers: a finish change (adding/removing rhodium or topcoat) alters corrosion resistance
a market requires a claimable corrosion certificate
field returns show tarnish or green skin staining

base.update_signal: a finish, claim-requirement, or return-pattern changes corrosion behaviour

nodes.definition: Define the wear/abrasion gate that decides whether the finish survives daily use. Methods: Taber rotary abraser (ASTM D4060, mass loss per 1000 cycles), reciprocating/rotating rub testers (Bass-type gold-wear class), and cheap screens (pencil-hardness ladder, 0000 steel-wool cycles, a fixed-load rub jig vs a retained standard) [FACT: method families]. Underpinning it is deposit hardness: soft (pure) gold ~60-90 HV vs hard (Co/Ni-alloyed) gold ~130-200 HV (ASTM B578 Knoop) [FACT], and H/E ratio as a wear predictor. Acceptance = no exposure of the underlayer/base metal at the agreed cycles versus a retained good part; a defined jig (fixed load, media, cycle count, never changed) beats no standard. Wear-through is decisive because it also opens nickel exposure and new corrosion pores.

included: soft vs hard gold hardness bands
no-underlayer-exposure acceptance vs a retained standard
excluded: the nickel-release consequence of wear-through (NICKEL_RELEASE_TEST)
the hardener chemistry itself (kb2)

pros.claim: Grading wear against a fixed jig and a retained standard turns a 'scratch-resistant' claim into a repeatable comparison
pros.example: a reciprocating-rub count to first underlayer exposure ranks a hard-gold finish above a soft-gold one objectively

cons.claim: In-house wear jigs are comparative only and silently change if the media/load/counter changes
cons.example: swapping the rub cloth brand alters the test and voids comparison to the retained standard

failure_modes: changing the jig media/load/cycle count so results are no longer comparable
grading gloss loss while ignoring the cycle at which the underlayer is first exposed
acceptance_tests: the Taber/reciprocating/pencil-hardness screens, the soft-vs-hard-gold hardness bands, and the no-underlayer-exposure acceptance vs a retained standard are stated
revisit_triggers: a hardener change (Co/Ni content) shifts deposit hardness
a quantified durability claim requires a Taber/Bass send-out
returns show wear-through at a service point

base.update_signal: a hardener, claim, or return-pattern changes wear behaviour

nodes.definition: Define the nickel-safety gate that is a legal pass/fail, not a marketing option, wherever the EU market applies. The dimethylglyoxime (DMG) spot test is a cheap qualitative nickel screen; the accredited gate is EN 1811, which measures released nickel with a limit of 0.5 ug/cm2/week for articles in prolonged skin contact and 0.2 ug/cm2/week for piercing posts, after EN 12472 wear-and-corrosion pre-conditioning that deliberately simulates worn plating exposing a nickel underlayer [FACT: REACH Annex XVII entry 27]. This gate matters acutely for the owner's 18-25 skin-contact audience. A nickel-free interlayer strategy (Pd, bronze, white bronze) is the compliant path when a nickel underlayer would otherwise be exposed by wear. Only the accredited EN 1811 certificate is a legal document; the DMG screen is not.

included: the DMG screen vs accredited EN 1811 gate
the 0.5 / 0.2 ug/cm2/week limits with EN 12472 pre-wear
excluded: the base-metal nickel content itself (kb1)
the wear test that exposes the nickel (WEAR_ABRASION_TEST)

pros.claim: Treating nickel release as a legal gate with a pre-wear step stops a compliant-when-new piece from failing once worn
pros.example: EN 12472 pre-conditioning before EN 1811 catches a nickel underlayer that only releases after the gold wears through

cons.claim: The accredited test is send-out and per-product, so it cannot gate every batch and the DMG screen is only qualitative
cons.example: a DMG-negative screen does not prove EN 1811 compliance for a label claim

failure_modes: treating a DMG-negative in-house screen as legal compliance
testing nickel release only on a new piece without EN 12472 pre-wear that a worn piece would fail
acceptance_tests: the DMG screen vs accredited EN 1811 gate, the 0.5/0.2 ug/cm2/week limits, EN 12472 pre-wear, and the nickel-free interlayer path are stated
revisit_triggers: the REACH nickel restriction or a target market's rule changes
a base metal or underlayer with nickel is introduced
a wear test shows the gold wearing through to a nickel layer

base.update_signal: a nickel regulation, base-metal, or wear-through change occurs

nodes.definition: Define the porosity gate, the decisive and most-missed failure mode of thin noble metal over an active base metal. Through-pores let a small-anode/large-cathode galvanic cell form in which the noble gold/rhodium cathode ACCELERATES corrosion of the exposed base metal at the pore [FACT: mechanism]. Screens: the ferroxyl test (potassium ferricyanide + NaCl gel/paper giving Prussian-blue spots at iron pores, ideal for a steel/iron core and bench-trivial) and ASTM B735 nitric-acid-vapor for gold over nickel [FACT]. Acceptance = pore count per cm2 within the agreed class, zero visible blue spots on ring wear surfaces at the 2.5 um class. Porosity falls steeply above ~1-2.5 um of noble metal [FACT: characteristic], so a passing-looking thin flash on steel is a corrosion time-bomb: this gate is why thickness cannot simply be minimised to save cost.

excluded: the corrosion-chamber tarnish test (TARNISH_CORROSION_TEST)
the base-metal nobility itself (kb1)

pros.claim: A cheap porosity screen exposes the pore-cell time-bomb that thickness-only and appearance grading both miss
pros.example: ferroxyl blue spots on a shiny thin-flash steel piece reveal pores that would rust in weeks

cons.claim: Porosity results are false if tested too soon (pores plugged with rinse residue) or only on proud surfaces
cons.example: a piece tested within hours of plating can read clean yet rust later once residue clears

failure_modes: skipping porosity and shipping a thin flash on an active base metal that rusts in service
testing porosity too soon after plating or only on proud surfaces, getting a false clean
acceptance_tests: the galvanic pore-cell mechanism, ferroxyl/nitric-vapor screens, the pore-count acceptance, and the steep thickness-porosity fall above ~1-2.5 um are stated
revisit_triggers: a thickness cost-down proposes going below the ~1-2.5 um porosity-safe band
the base metal changes to a more active core
returns show pitting or rust spots

base.update_signal: a thickness cut, base-metal change, or rust-return signal occurs

nodes.definition: Assemble the individual test gates into one acceptance plan with two layers. Pre-production qualification (once per product/process/bath change): plate flat witness coupons and offcuts alongside real parts in the same rack position, run the full battery in sequence (thickness -> adhesion -> forming -> porosity -> corrosion/sweat -> wear -> nickel), against WRITTEN numeric pass/fail criteria set before testing, and require three consecutive conforming lots before scale-up [FACT: QC practice]. Per-batch routine (after qualification): 100% visual at 10x, XRF first-article + sampling (AQL / ISO 2859-1 attribute plan or sqrt(N)+1), one wrap-bend witness, a ferroxyl spot-check, and color vs a retained master panel, with a batch record row filled BEFORE parts move to stock. Criteria invented after seeing results always pass; witnesses that did not ride with the lot do not represent it.

included: witness coupons, worst-case specimens, written criteria, three-lot rule, AQL sampling
excluded: which subset gates the high-quality claim (GRADE_GATE_MAP)
the cost of running the plan (COST_DRIVERS)

pros.claim: A two-layer plan with witnesses and pre-written criteria makes the grade repeatable and drift-detectable at low cost
pros.example: a per-batch color-panel + ferroxyl check catches process drift long before a full re-qualification is due

cons.claim: The per-batch routine is the recurring cost that gets skipped first under deadline pressure
cons.example: dropping the 15-45 min batch record turns a later return into an unsolvable mystery

failure_modes: inventing acceptance criteria after seeing the results
plating witness coupons separately so they do not represent the true bath/rack condition
acceptance_tests: the qualification (witnesses, worst-case specimens, written criteria, three-lot, AQL) and per-batch routine with record-before-stock are stated
revisit_triggers: a bath make-up, target, base-metal or wire lot changes (requalification trigger)
a long stoppage or process relocation occurs
the AQL/sampling requirement changes

base.update_signal: a requalification trigger or a sampling-requirement change occurs

nodes.definition: Map which acceptance tests must pass to earn 'high-quality' and each label claim, so the grade is auditable. The gate set is sized to claim and duty: a label word ('gold electroplate', 'heavy gold electroplate', 'vermeil') is gated by the thickness/fineness measurement; a 'tarnish-resistant' claim is gated by the corrosion/sweat test (accredited if printed); a 'hypoallergenic/nickel-safe' claim is gated by accredited EN 1811 with EN 12472 pre-wear; a wear/'scratch-resistant' claim is gated by the wear test vs a retained standard; and any piece over an active base metal is gated by porosity and adhesion regardless of claim [FACT/METHOD]. High-quality = clears every gate its claim and wear duty require at the worst-case point. In-house screens gate process release; accredited results gate the legal/marketing claim. This node is the direct answer to 'which acceptance tests gate high-quality'.

included: the always-on porosity+adhesion gates over active base metal
excluded: the test procedures themselves (the test nodes)
the cost-quality tradeoff (COST_QUALITY_CURVE)

pros.claim: Mapping each claim to its gating test makes 'high-quality' and every label word individually defensible
pros.example: a 'nickel-safe' claim released only on an accredited EN 1811 certificate, not a DMG screen, is audit-proof

cons.claim: A claim-sized gate map means more claims require more accredited tests, raising the cost of a bigger promise
cons.example: adding 'tarnish-resistant' and 'nickel-safe' to a label pulls in two send-out certificates

failure_modes: making a claim whose gating test was never run (e.g. 'tarnish-free' with no corrosion test)
gating a printed legal claim on an in-house screen instead of an accredited result
acceptance_tests: the claim-to-gate mapping, the always-on porosity+adhesion gates, and the screen-vs-accredited claim split are stated as the high-quality definition
revisit_triggers: a new label or marketing claim is added
a regulation changes which test gates a claim
a market requires accreditation for a previously in-house-gated claim

base.update_signal: a new claim or a regulation changes the gate map

nodes.definition: Enumerate what actually drives the cost of quality in a plated piece, so value engineering targets the right lever. The drivers [METHOD/FACT]: noble-metal micron consumption (gold and, for white finishes, rhodium, priced per micron over the significant surface, the single largest and most price-volatile driver); the underlayer stack (sulfamate-nickel leveling/hardening coat, Pd or white-bronze barrier); the hardener system (Co/Ni for hard gold); labor and QC time per piece (15-45 min per batch of routine testing, the recurring cost skipped first); destructive-test material burn (witness coupons, stripped spots); and accredited send-out tests amortized once per product/process, not per batch. Metal price is a genuine [UNKNOWN] forward and must be re-pulled, never guessed. This driver stack is the input to the cost-quality curve and every VE lever.

included: noble-metal micron, underlayer, hardener, labor/QC, test-burn, send-out amortization drivers
excluded: the retail price built on the COGS (economics specialist)
the curve shape those drivers produce (COST_QUALITY_CURVE)

pros.claim: Naming the driver stack shows where cost really sits (micron + underlayer + QC time) so VE targets a real lever not a rounding error
pros.example: recognising gold micron as the dominant driver points VE at thickness placement rather than shaving cheap consumables

cons.claim: The dominant driver (metal price) is a forward [UNKNOWN], so any absolute cost figure is a re-pull-and-recompute, not a fixed number
cons.example: a gold price move re-ranks whether thickness tuning or batch economics is the bigger saving

failure_modes: optimising a trivial consumable while the gold-micron and QC-time drivers dominate the cost
hardening a metal-price figure into a fixed COGS instead of tagging it a re-pulled [UNKNOWN]
acceptance_tests: the noble-metal-micron, underlayer, hardener, labor/QC, test-burn and send-out drivers are enumerated with metal price flagged a re-pulled [UNKNOWN]
revisit_triggers: the gold/rhodium price moves materially
a QC step is added or removed changing labor time
a send-out test is added, changing per-product amortization

base.update_signal: a metal-price, QC-step, or send-out change moves the driver stack

nodes.definition: Model the cost-vs-quality relationship as a diminishing-returns curve, not a line [METHOD/ESTIMATE]. Below a floor (e.g. a sub-porosity-safe flash on steel, a missing nickel barrier, a below-label-class thickness) the piece fails a gate and is worth nothing however shiny; through a working band each added micron, hardener or barrier buys real gate margin; above a knee, extra gold micron and extra testing buy mostly perceived quality and little added real durability. The value-engineering target is the knee: trim over-spec above it without dropping below any gate, and never buy down toward the floor. The curve's exact position is product-specific and metal-price-dependent [ESTIMATE], so it is drawn per product from the driver stack and the gate map, not asserted as universal.

included: the knee as the VE target
excluded: the specific levers that move along the curve (the VE nodes)
the price charged for a given quality (economics specialist)

pros.claim: A floor-and-knee curve tells VE exactly where cutting cost is free (above the knee) and where it destroys the product (below a gate)
pros.example: trimming gold micron from well above the wear knee saves cost with no gate loss, unlike trimming toward the porosity floor

cons.claim: The curve's position is an [ESTIMATE] that moves with product and metal price, so it guides direction not an exact spend
cons.example: a rhodium price spike shifts the knee for a white finish and re-opens the tradeoff

failure_modes: treating cost and quality as linear and shaving uniformly into a gate
confusing above-knee perceived-quality spend with below-floor real-quality spend and cutting the wrong one
acceptance_tests: the floor/working-band/knee curve shape, the knee as the VE target, and its product-and-price-specific [ESTIMATE] positioning are stated
revisit_triggers: the metal price or a cost driver moves the knee
a gate threshold changes moving the floor
a new product with a different wear duty needs its own curve

base.update_signal: a metal-price, gate-threshold, or new-product change shifts the curve

nodes.definition: The base-metal lever: choose the cheapest substrate that still clears the nickel and porosity gates for the piece's duty [METHOD]. The tradeoff space (properties owned by kb1): brass is cheap and workable but tarnish-prone and often nickel-bearing; sterling 925 is a premium base that enables 'vermeil' when gold-plated >=2.5um; 316L stainless is durable and skin-friendly but harder to plate; zinc/pewter alloys are cheapest for cast pieces but soft. Value engineering picks down the cost ladder only until a gate binds: a cheaper nickel-bearing base is acceptable ONLY behind a compliant nickel-free barrier that keeps EN 1811 within limits even after EN 12472 wear pre-conditioning [FACT: the limit binds]. Base metal is a lever, not a free choice: the nickel-release gate and the porosity gate constrain how far down the cost ladder it can go.

included: the brass/925/316L/zinc cost-vs-gate tradeoff as a lever
the nickel-free-barrier condition on a cheaper nickel-bearing base
vermeil-enabling role of a sterling base
excluded: the base-metal metallurgy itself (kb1)
the barrier-layer engineering detail (VE_BARRIER_LAYERS)

pros.claim: Choosing the cheapest gate-passing base metal is a large cost lever that need not touch perceived quality
pros.example: a brass base behind a compliant barrier can match a pricier base on appearance while cutting substrate cost

cons.claim: A cheaper nickel-bearing base raises compliance risk and may need a barrier that erodes part of the saving
cons.example: the barrier and extra EN 1811 testing needed to make cheap brass compliant offset some of the substrate saving

failure_modes: dropping to a cheaper nickel-bearing base without a barrier, failing EN 1811 after wear
using a base metal too active for the target thickness, failing porosity
acceptance_tests: the base-metal cost-vs-gate tradeoff, the nickel-free-barrier condition on a nickel-bearing base, and the sterling-enables-vermeil point are stated
revisit_triggers: a base-metal price change re-ranks the ladder
the nickel or porosity gate tightens
a new piece duty (ring vs earring) changes the acceptable base

base.update_signal: a base-metal price or a nickel/porosity gate change occurs

nodes.definition: The thickness lever: place noble-metal micron where wear and porosity demand it and thin it where they do not, rather than plating uniformly thick [METHOD]. Significant-surface engineering puts the class thickness (e.g. >=2.5 um for a ring wear surface) on the high-wear, skin-contact and visible zones while allowing a thinner but still porosity-safe deposit in hidden recesses, cutting gold consumption without dropping any gate. The hard constraints: never below the FTC class the label claims, and never below the ~1-2.5 um porosity-safe band over an active base metal [FACT]. This is a real cost-down because gold micron is the dominant driver, but it lives entirely above the floor: thinning into the porosity or label gate is not value engineering, it is a defect.

included: the label-class and porosity-safe floors as hard limits
excluded: the plating process that controls thickness distribution (kb2)
the barrier that lets thinner gold survive (VE_BARRIER_LAYERS)

pros.claim: Selective thickness placement cuts the dominant gold-micron cost while every wear/porosity/label gate still passes
pros.example: class thickness on the ring face and a thinner porosity-safe deposit inside the band saves gold with no gate loss

cons.claim: Selective placement needs process control over thickness distribution and worst-case-point verification, or it drifts below a floor
cons.example: a low-current-density recess can end up below the porosity-safe band if distribution is not measured

failure_modes: thinning uniformly into the FTC class or the porosity-safe band to save gold
assuming even distribution and not measuring the low-current-density worst-case point
acceptance_tests: significant-surface selective placement, the label-class and porosity-safe floors, and gold-micron saving as the value are stated
revisit_triggers: a gold price change alters the saving from thinning
a label class or porosity floor changes the minimum
a wear test shows the thinned zone wearing through

base.update_signal: a gold-price, floor, or wear-through change alters the thickness lever

nodes.definition: The barrier-layer lever, the classic move that lowers cost and RAISES durability at once [METHOD/FACT]. A hard sulfamate-nickel or Pd/white-bronze underlayer (HV ~200-400) levels the substrate, resists wear, and load-supports a THINNER gold that then survives the wear gate it could not survive alone; a Pd or white-bronze barrier blocks base-metal diffusion and tarnish and can be nickel-free for compliance; an e-coat/cataphoretic or nano-ceramic clear topcoat (and, for white finishes, hard rhodium) adds tarnish and abrasion resistance over a thinner precious layer. The net: barrier architecture cuts the expensive gold micron while lifting the wear and corrosion grades, so it moves the whole cost-quality curve favourably rather than sliding along it. The constraint: the duplex hardness rule (coating no harder than its support allows) and the added barrier/topcoat cost must still net a saving.

included: hard-underlayer load-support letting thinner gold pass the wear gate
topcoat/rhodium over a thinner precious layer
excluded: the barrier deposition chemistry (kb2)
the base-metal choice underneath (VE_BASE_METAL)

pros.claim: Barrier architecture is the rare lever that cuts gold cost and raises the wear/corrosion grade simultaneously
pros.example: a hard Ni underlayer lets a thinner gold pass the wear test it would fail unsupported, saving gold and improving durability

cons.claim: The barrier and topcoat add their own cost and process steps, and a nickel barrier reopens the nickel-release gate if exposed by wear
cons.example: a nickel underlayer that wears through must still pass EN 1811, or a nickel-free barrier must replace it

failure_modes: deleting the underlayer to save a step, losing leveling/wear support and exposing tarnish
adding a nickel barrier that a worn piece exposes above the EN 1811 limit
acceptance_tests: the hard-underlayer load-support, the Pd/white-bronze diffusion/nickel-compliant barrier, and the topcoat/rhodium-over-thinner-gold levers are stated with the duplex and net-saving constraints
revisit_triggers: a wear or corrosion test result changes the barrier need
a nickel-compliance issue forces a nickel-free barrier
the barrier/topcoat cost changes the net saving

base.update_signal: a wear/corrosion result, nickel-compliance, or barrier-cost change occurs

nodes.definition: The finish-system lever: match the finish to the price tier and the durability the claim actually needs, not to maximal prestige [METHOD]. The menu (chemistry owned by kb2): gold plating / vermeil / gold-filled for warm tones; rhodium over sterling silver or white gold for a bright-white, hard, tarnish-resistant finish; PVD 'gold/ion plating' for a hard thin decorative layer; e-coat topcoat for cheap added protection. Value engineering asks which finish clears the required gates at least cost: rhodium buys real tarnish and wear resistance (worth it on a white-finish piece that must stay bright) but is a platinum-group metal with a volatile price, so specifying rhodium where a cheaper protected finish would pass the same gates is over-spec above the knee. Finish is chosen to the gate and the tier, and its durability contribution is verified, not assumed from its prestige.

included: gold/vermeil/rhodium/PVD/e-coat finish menu as a lever
matching finish to gate and price tier
excluded: the finish deposition science (kb2)
the barrier/topcoat under the finish (VE_BARRIER_LAYERS)

pros.claim: Choosing the finish to the gate and tier avoids paying for prestige metal that buys no extra passed gate
pros.example: a protected gold finish that passes the same tarnish gate as rhodium at lower cost is the value-engineered choice for a warm-tone tier

cons.claim: Down-specifying the finish can cut real durability if the cheaper finish quietly fails a gate the prestige finish passed
cons.example: dropping rhodium on a white-finish piece may fail the tarnish gate that only rhodium/topcoat cleared

failure_modes: specifying rhodium (volatile PGM price) where a cheaper protected finish passes the same gates
down-specifying to a cheaper finish that fails the tarnish/wear gate the prestige finish passed
acceptance_tests: the finish menu as a lever, matching finish to gate and tier, and rhodium's real-durability-but-volatile-price framing are stated
revisit_triggers: the rhodium/gold price changes the finish tradeoff
a tarnish/wear test shows a finish failing its gate
a price tier or color direction changes the target finish

base.update_signal: a metal-price, gate-result, or tier change alters the finish choice

nodes.definition: The batch/run-economics lever: spread the fixed costs of plating and testing over the run without dropping per-batch drift control [METHOD]. Levers: barrel vs rack plating and rack utilization (fill the bath and the run), batch size to amortize setup and the once-per-product accredited send-out tests over more pieces, and consolidating QC destructive-test burn onto shared witness coupons. The saving is real because labor/QC time and send-out amortization are meaningful drivers, but the hard limit is the per-batch routine that catches drift: color-vs-master-panel, first-article XRF, a wrap-bend witness and a ferroxyl spot-check must survive any batch-size increase, because color drift is the earliest alarm and skipping it converts a later return into an unsolvable mystery [FACT: practice]. Bigger batches amortize fixed cost; they do not license skipping the per-batch gate.

included: barrel/rack utilization and batch-size amortization of setup + send-out tests
the per-batch drift-control floor that survives scale-up
excluded: the working-capital cost of bigger inventory (economics specialist)
the individual tests being amortized (ACCEPTANCE_TEST_PLAN)

pros.claim: Amortizing setup and once-per-product send-out tests over a bigger run cuts per-piece cost with no quality change
pros.example: one accredited EN 1811 certificate spread over a larger product run lowers per-piece test cost without touching the grade

cons.claim: Batch-size gains tempt dropping per-batch QC, which surfaces later as an undetected drift shipping to customers
cons.example: a larger batch that skips the color-panel check ships a whole batch of drifted color before anyone notices

failure_modes: increasing batch size and dropping the per-batch color/XRF/ferroxyl checks
amortizing an accredited test across product changes it no longer represents
acceptance_tests: the barrel/rack utilization, batch-size amortization, shared-witness burn levers and the surviving per-batch drift-control floor are stated
revisit_triggers: batch volume crosses a threshold changing the in-house-vs-send-out balance
a process change invalidates the amortized send-out test
a drift escapes a scaled-up batch

base.update_signal: a batch-volume, process, or drift-escape change alters batch economics

nodes.definition: Separate perceived quality (what a buyer senses without a lab: color/shade per NIHS 1N-3N, gloss, heft, finish uniformity, packaging) from real quality (what the acceptance battery measures: adhesion, worst-case thickness, porosity, corrosion, wear, nickel-safety) [METHOD]. The value-engineering opportunity is precise: cost may be cut on real over-spec that sits ABOVE the knee and is invisible to the buyer (e.g. gold micron beyond the wear gate) without touching perceived quality; and perceived quality can sometimes be RAISED cheaply (better color control, heft, packaging) to support a price. The trap is the inverse: cutting real quality below a gate while preserving the perceived-quality illusion, which ships a piece that looks premium and fails in weeks. Perceived and real quality are managed separately, and real quality is never traded below a gate to fund a perceived-quality look.

included: cutting invisible above-knee over-spec without touching perceived quality
never trading real quality below a gate for a perceived look
excluded: the pricing built on perceived value (economics specialist)
the specific gate tests (the test nodes)

pros.claim: Separating perceived from real quality shows exactly where cost-down is safe (invisible over-spec) and where it is fraud (below a gate)
pros.example: trimming invisible above-knee gold saves cost safely while a heavier box lifts perceived quality, neither touching a gate

cons.claim: Perceived quality can mask a real-quality cut long enough to damage the brand before returns reveal it
cons.example: a premium-looking piece that fails porosity ships and only surfaces as rust weeks later

failure_modes: funding a perceived-quality look (weight, packaging) by cutting a real-durability gate
assuming perceived quality signals real quality and skipping the gate tests
acceptance_tests: the perceived/real split, safe above-knee cost-down, and the never-trade-real-below-a-gate rule are stated
revisit_triggers: a cost-down proposal touches a real-quality gate
a perceived-quality change (color, weight, packaging) is proposed
returns reveal a real-quality failure behind a premium look

base.update_signal: a cost-down, perceived-quality, or return signal touches the split

nodes.definition: Catalogue the cost-downs that cross a quality gate and are therefore quality cuts, not value engineering [METHOD/FACT]. The recurring traps: thinning noble metal below the ~1-2.5 um porosity-safe band on an active base metal (a corrosion time-bomb that passes visual); deleting the nickel/barrier underlayer to save a step (loses leveling/wear support and exposes tarnish and, if nickel, the EN 1811 limit); dropping to a cheaper nickel-bearing base without a compliant barrier (fails nickel release after EN 12472 wear); skipping the per-batch QC to save time (ships drift); and quoting in-house-screen results as accredited claims. Each looks like a saving on a spreadsheet and is a defect or a legal exposure in the field. The discriminator is simple: if the cost-down changes what the piece can pass, it crossed a gate and is out of bounds.

included: the 'changes what it can pass' discriminator
excluded: the legitimate above-knee levers (the VE nodes)
the decision procedure that enforces the boundary (VE_DECISION_PROTOCOL)

pros.claim: A named catalogue of false economies lets a cost-down be screened against known gate-crossings before it ships
pros.example: a proposal to thin flash on steel is flagged against the porosity trap before it becomes a rust-return wave

cons.claim: The catalogue is a checklist of known traps and cannot anticipate every novel gate-crossing
cons.example: a new finish could introduce a failure mode not yet in the list

failure_modes: accepting a spreadsheet saving that quietly drops a gate (porosity, nickel, adhesion)
quoting an in-house screen as an accredited claim to avoid a send-out cost
acceptance_tests: the gate-crossing catalogue and the 'changes what it can pass' discriminator are stated with the field-defect framing
revisit_triggers: a new cost-down proposal is screened
a new finish or process adds a possible gate-crossing
a field return traces to a false economy

base.update_signal: a new cost-down, finish, or return traces to a gate-crossing

nodes.definition: The value-engineering decision procedure that ties the levers, the curve and the gate into one repeatable loop [METHOD]. Steps: (1) fix the acceptance gate for the product from GRADE_GATE_MAP and hold it constant; (2) draw the cost-quality curve from the current driver stack and locate the knee; (3) move ONE lever at a time (base metal, thickness placement, barrier architecture, finish, batch economics) toward the knee; (4) re-run the SAME acceptance battery on witnesses of the changed spec; (5) accept the cost-down only if it re-passes every gate at the worst-case point, else reject it as a quality cut. One lever at a time keeps cause and effect legible; re-testing the same battery is what distinguishes value engineering from a quality cut. The output is a lower-cost spec proven to hold the same graded quality.

included: the hold-gate / one-lever / re-test / accept-if-passes loop
excluded: the price set on the cost-engineered spec (economics specialist)
the individual lever mechanics (the VE nodes)

pros.claim: A hold-gate/move-one-lever/re-test loop makes every cost-down provable rather than hopeful
pros.example: moving only the underlayer and re-running the wear+nickel battery proves a thinner gold still passes before it ships

cons.claim: One-lever-at-a-time re-testing is slower than changing several inputs at once
cons.example: a maker under deadline may want to change base metal and thickness together and skip the re-test

failure_modes: moving several levers at once so a failed re-test cannot be attributed
accepting a cost-down without re-running the same battery on the changed spec
acceptance_tests: the hold-gate / one-lever / re-test-same-battery / accept-only-if-passes loop and the proven lower-cost-same-quality output are stated
revisit_triggers: a new cost-down lever is proposed
the gate set changes, requiring a re-run
a metal-price move re-locates the knee

base.update_signal: a new lever, gate change, or price move re-runs the protocol

nodes.definition: Enforce the honesty discipline across the grading and value-engineering work so claims are trusted and screens are not over-read. Solid [FACT] (cited, load-bearing): the FTC thickness/label ladder and vermeil=sterling-base rule; the ASTM B571 adhesion battery; ISO 9227/ASTM B117 salt spray; ASTM D4060 Taber wear; EN 1811 limits (0.5/0.2 ug/cm2/week) with EN 12472 pre-wear; the ferroxyl/ASTM B735 porosity methods and the galvanic pore-cell mechanism; rhodium as a hard, bright, tarnish-resistant platinum-group metal. Soft [ESTIMATE/METHOD/UNKNOWN]: the cost-quality curve position and knee ([ESTIMATE], product-and-price-specific); the forward gold/rhodium price ([UNKNOWN], re-pull never guess); every in-house-screen result (comparative, NOT accredited); heat-quench/sweat handbook temperatures and durations ([ESTIMATE]). The binding rule: never quote a screen-grade result as an accredited [FACT], and never state a market number (share, price, demographic rate) this KB does not measure.

included: the [FACT] standard/mechanism anchors vs the [ESTIMATE]/[METHOD]/[UNKNOWN] soft inputs
excluded: the substantive test/lever content (the other nodes)
the market-measurement methods themselves (market specialist)

pros.claim: A single ledger separating cited standards from screen-grade estimates keeps every quality claim defensible
pros.example: tagging EN 1811 limits [FACT] but an in-house DMG screen [ESTIMATE] tells a reader exactly what is claimable

cons.claim: Heavy tagging can read as hedging when a stakeholder wants a single hard number the evidence does not support
cons.example: a buyer wanting one COGS or one 'grade' must accept a band and a set of gate passes instead

failure_modes: quoting an in-house screen result as an accredited legal claim
hardening the forward metal price or a curve knee into a fake-precise number
acceptance_tests: the [FACT] anchors, the [ESTIMATE]/[METHOD]/[UNKNOWN] soft inputs, the screen-not-accredited rule, and the no-invented-market-numbers rule are enumerated
revisit_triggers: a screen result is upgraded by an accredited send-out
a [FACT] standard or limit is revised
a forward metal price becomes known

base.update_signal: a screen upgrade, standard revision, or known price changes the ledger

nodes.definition: Compose the segment's hand-off: deliver a graded, cost-engineered product spec and stop cleanly before pricing and assortment. The spec carries, per piece: the base metal + underlayer/barrier + finish + significant-surface thickness callout; the acceptance gates it passed (thickness class, adhesion, porosity, corrosion, wear, nickel) at the worst-case point, with screen-vs-accredited status flagged; and the value-engineering levers applied with their proven same-gate result. This KB owns whether a piece is honestly high-quality and how to make it cheaper without dropping that grade; it does NOT own the retail price, keystone/contribution math, or the launch assortment (the economics and assortment specialists). Binding conditions passed on: re-pull the metal price before any COGS; re-run the acceptance battery on any lever change; gate every printed claim on an accredited result; and never ship a piece that fails a gate at the worst-case point.

included: the graded cost-engineered spec output (metal/underlayer/finish/thickness + passed gates + levers)
the binding conditions passed to downstream specialists
excluded: the retail price and contribution math (economics specialist)
the launch six-SKU assortment (assortment specialist)

pros.claim: A clean hand-off delivers a provably graded, cost-engineered spec and names the conditions without overstepping into pricing
pros.example: passing a spec with its passed gates plus a re-pull-metal-price condition lets economics build a defensible COGS

cons.claim: The spec carries screen-vs-accredited status and a re-pull price condition, so downstream inherits a conditional COGS not a fixed one
cons.example: economics must re-pull the gold price and confirm accredited claims before quoting a price

failure_modes: letting the graded spec drift into a pricing verdict this KB does not own
handing off a spec without its screen-vs-accredited status or the re-test-on-lever-change condition
acceptance_tests: the graded cost-engineered spec, the passed gates at the worst-case point, the clean pre-pricing boundary, and the four binding conditions are stated
revisit_triggers: a lever change requires re-running the battery
the economics specialist requests a tighter or accredited-only spec
a gate result or metal price changes the spec

base.update_signal: a lever change, downstream request, or gate/price change updates the hand-off

require the accredited certificate for the claim
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: gate process release on the in-house screen but gate every printed claim (nickel, tarnish, thickness/karat) on an accredited result

conflict_axes.name: speed_to_market_vs_qualification_rigor
conflict_axes.description: Skipping the three-lot pre-production qualification launches faster but ships an ungraded, drift-prone product.
poles: launch fast on a partial qualification
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: require the full witnessed qualification and three conforming lots before scale-up; a faster launch on an unqualified process is a hidden defect risk

conflict_axes.name: finish_prestige_vs_durability_cost
conflict_axes.description: A prestige finish (rhodium/PVD) signals quality but may cost more than the durability the claim actually needs, or a cheaper finish may fail the gate the prestige one passed.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: choose the finish that passes the required tarnish/wear gate at least cost; verify a down-specified finish re-passes the gate before accepting it

edge_cases.description: A too-thin gold flash on an active base metal passes visual inspection but is a corrosion time-bomb once porosity opens the galvanic pore cell
edge_cases.trigger: a thickness cost-down goes below the ~1-2.5 um porosity-safe band without a porosity test
edge_cases.mitigation: hold the porosity-safe band as a hard floor and run ferroxyl on worst-case zones >=24 h after plating before release

edge_cases.description: Wear-through exposes a nickel underlayer and pushes nickel release above the 0.5 ug/cm2/week limit even though the new piece passed
edge_cases.trigger: a worn piece over a nickel underlayer is tested without EN 12472 wear pre-conditioning
edge_cases.mitigation: run EN 1811 after EN 12472 pre-wear, or use a nickel-free barrier so wear-through stays compliant

edge_cases.description: An XRF calibrated on the wrong stack reads thickness 2-3x off and passes an out-of-class piece or fails a good one
edge_cases.trigger: a wrong-stack calibration foil (e.g. Au-on-brass for an Au-on-Ni-on-steel part) is used
edge_cases.mitigation: calibrate on the exact Au/Ni/base stack and cross-check with coulometric on a witness

edge_cases.description: Cohesive hairline cracking of hard gold at a tight bend is misread as an adhesion-failure reject, scrapping a good lot
edge_cases.trigger: a bend test on hard gold is inspected at low magnification without failure-mode discrimination
edge_cases.mitigation: inspect at 10x: cracks with no lifting are cohesive (accept); flakes exposing the underlayer are adhesive (reject and audit prep)

edge_cases.description: A base-metal-core piece is labeled 'vermeil', which is reserved for a sterling-silver base with >=2.5 um gold
edge_cases.trigger: a gold-over-brass or gold-over-steel piece is marked vermeil
edge_cases.mitigation: reserve 'vermeil' for a sterling base + >=2.5 um gold; use 'heavy gold electroplate' for a base-metal core at that thickness

edge_cases.description: Salt-spray hours are quoted from a non-conformant DIY fog box as if claimable
edge_cases.trigger: in-house fog-box results are printed on a label or spec as a corrosion claim
edge_cases.mitigation: use the fog box for comparative screening only and source printed corrosion claims from an accredited conformant chamber

edge_cases.description: A batch-size increase drops the per-batch color-panel check and a whole batch of drifted color ships
edge_cases.trigger: batch economics removes the per-batch QC to cut time
edge_cases.mitigation: keep the per-batch color/XRF/wrap-bend/ferroxyl floor regardless of batch size; color drift is the earliest alarm

edge_cases.description: Deleting the nickel/barrier underlayer to save a step loses leveling and wear support and exposes tarnish and nickel
edge_cases.trigger: the underlayer is removed as a cost-down without re-testing wear/corrosion/nickel
edge_cases.mitigation: treat the underlayer as load-bearing; re-run wear, corrosion and nickel before accepting its removal

edge_cases.description: A 'tarnish-free' or 'scratch-resistant' marketing claim is made with no substantiating test behind it
edge_cases.trigger: a durability claim is printed without a gating corrosion or wear test
edge_cases.mitigation: gate every durability claim on its test (accredited if printed); drop unsubstantiated 'tarnish-free' language

edge_cases.description: A value-engineered cost-down is accepted without re-running the same acceptance battery on the changed spec
edge_cases.trigger: a lever is moved and the piece ships on the old qualification
edge_cases.mitigation: re-run the same battery on witnesses of the changed spec and accept only if every gate re-passes at the worst-case point

edge_cases.description: A perceived-quality upgrade (heavier weight, better box) masks a real-durability downgrade below a gate
edge_cases.trigger: a finish or thickness cost-down is hidden behind packaging/heft while a gate is dropped
edge_cases.mitigation: manage perceived and real quality separately; never fund a perceived-quality look by dropping a real-quality gate

workflow.action: Define the quality grade as a gate-set
workflow.description: State the six quality dimensions sized to the piece's label claim and wear duty, graded at the worst-case point
workflow.gate: the six dimensions, worst-case-point rule and claim/duty sizing are stated

workflow.action: Set the thickness/label gate and measurement
workflow.description: Fix the FTC flash/GEP/HGE/vermeil ladder and worst-case-point XRF+coulometric measurement
workflow.gate: the FTC ladder, worst-case measurement and never-vermeil-on-base-metal rule are stated

workflow.description: Run B571 wrap/tape/heat-quench and discriminate cohesive cracking from adhesive peel
workflow.gate: the B571 battery and cohesive-vs-adhesive discrimination are stated

workflow.action: Run the corrosion, sweat and porosity screens
workflow.description: Run salt-spray/sweat corrosion and ferroxyl porosity screens and note the rhodium/barrier mechanism
workflow.gate: the corrosion/sweat screens, porosity gate and in-house-vs-accredited split are stated

workflow.action: Run the wear and nickel gates
workflow.description: Run the wear/abrasion screen vs a retained standard and the DMG/EN 1811 nickel gate with EN 12472 pre-wear
workflow.gate: the wear screen, the no-underlayer-exposure acceptance and the nickel limits are stated

workflow.description: Combine the tests into a witnessed qualification (three lots, written criteria, AQL) plus a per-batch routine
workflow.gate: the qualification and per-batch routine with record-before-stock are stated

workflow.description: Map each label/durability claim to its gating test and the always-on porosity+adhesion gates
workflow.gate: the claim-to-gate mapping and screen-vs-accredited claim split are stated

workflow.description: Draw the floor/working-band/knee curve from the driver stack and the gate floors
workflow.gate: the floor/knee curve shape and the knee as the VE target are stated

workflow.description: Move base-metal, thickness, barrier, finish and batch levers toward the knee, one at a time
workflow.gate: each lever states its cost-down and the gate it must still pass

workflow.description: Screen each cost-down against the gate-crossing catalogue and reject any that changes what the piece passes
workflow.gate: the gate-crossing catalogue and the 'changes what it can pass' discriminator are applied

workflow.action: Run the VE decision loop and hand off
workflow.description: Hold the gate, move one lever, re-run the same battery, accept if it passes, and hand off the graded cost-engineered spec with its conditions
workflow.gate: the proven lower-cost-same-quality spec, its passed gates and the binding conditions are stated

dominance_rules.rule: The label/legality gate dominates any thickness cost-down
dominance_rules.rationale: a below-class thickness or a 'vermeil' claim on a base-metal core is a mislabel regardless of the saving
dominance_rules.trigger: a cost-down proposes a thickness below the claimed FTC class or a reserved label word
dominance_rules.action: hold the class thickness at the worst-case point and use only a label the measured thickness/base supports

dominance_rules.rule: The nickel-release limit dominates any base-metal cost saving
dominance_rules.rationale: EN 1811 (0.5/0.2 ug/cm2/week) is pass/fail law where sold, not a marketing option
dominance_rules.trigger: a cheaper nickel-bearing base or a nickel barrier is proposed
dominance_rules.action: require a compliant nickel-free barrier proven under EN 12472 pre-wear, else choose a compliant base

dominance_rules.rule: The porosity/corrosion gate dominates thinning gold over an active base metal
dominance_rules.rationale: porosity opens a galvanic pore cell in which the noble coating accelerates base-metal corrosion
dominance_rules.trigger: a thickness cut approaches the ~1-2.5 um porosity-safe band on an active base metal
dominance_rules.action: hold the porosity-safe floor and verify with ferroxyl on worst-case zones before release

dominance_rules.rule: The same acceptance battery dominates any value-engineering cost-down
dominance_rules.rationale: a cost-down that is not re-tested on the changed spec is unproven and may have dropped a gate
dominance_rules.trigger: a lever is moved to cut cost
dominance_rules.action: re-run the same battery on witnesses of the changed spec and accept only if every gate re-passes

dominance_rules.rationale: a premium-looking piece that fails a gate still fails in the field and damages the brand
dominance_rules.trigger: a cost-down preserves the look while dropping a real-quality gate
dominance_rules.action: never trade a real-quality gate for a perceived-quality look; keep the two managed separately

dominance_rules.rule: The accredited result dominates the in-house screen for any printed claim
dominance_rules.rationale: in-house screens are comparative and not legally claimable
dominance_rules.trigger: a nickel, tarnish, thickness or karat claim is printed
dominance_rules.action: gate the printed claim on an accredited certificate; use the in-house screen only for process release

dominance_rules.rule: The worst-case-point measurement dominates the average
dominance_rules.rationale: a plated piece fails at its thinnest, lowest-current-density point, not its proud average
dominance_rules.trigger: a grade is read on the proud surface average
dominance_rules.action: measure and grade the recess/inside-band/high-wear worst-case point

dominance_rules.rule: Adhesive-failure discrimination dominates a raw crack count in the reject decision
dominance_rules.rationale: cohesive hard-gold cracking is expected while adhesive peel is a true defect
dominance_rules.action: inspect at 10x and reject only on lifting/peel exposing the underlayer, not on cohesive cracks

dominance_rules.rule: Per-batch drift control dominates batch-size cost savings
dominance_rules.rationale: color drift is the earliest failure alarm and precedes thickness/adhesion failures by many batches
dominance_rules.trigger: a batch-size increase proposes dropping the per-batch checks
dominance_rules.action: keep the per-batch color/XRF/wrap-bend/ferroxyl floor regardless of batch size

anti_rework_rules.rule: Write numeric acceptance criteria before running any test
anti_rework_rules.prevents: criteria invented after seeing results that always pass and must later be defended or retracted

anti_rework_rules.rule: Plate flat witness coupons and offcuts with every qualification lot in the same rack position
anti_rework_rules.prevents: destructive tests consuming sellable parts and witnesses that do not represent the true bath/rack condition

anti_rework_rules.rule: Calibrate XRF on the exact Au/Ni/base stack before measuring thickness
anti_rework_rules.prevents: confidently-wrong thickness readings that pass an out-of-class piece or fail a good one

anti_rework_rules.rule: Hold the acceptance gate constant and move one value-engineering lever at a time, re-testing only the changed spec
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a multi-lever change whose failed re-test cannot be attributed, forcing a full re-qualification

anti_rework_rules.rule: Send out EN 1811 and conformant salt-spray once per product/process, not per batch, and re-pull only on a process change
anti_rework_rules.prevents: either per-batch send-out cost or an amortized certificate applied to a product it no longer represents

anti_rework_rules.rule: Match the base metal and underlayer to the nickel and porosity gates before pricing the piece
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a priced spec that later fails nickel or porosity and must be re-engineered after quoting

anti_rework_rules.rule: Place class thickness on the significant surface at design time, not after returns
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a uniform-thickness over-spend or an under-spent wear point discovered only as field wear-through

anti_rework_rules.rule: Distinguish cohesive from adhesive failure during qualification, documented with photos
anti_rework_rules.prevents: good lots scrapped for cohesive cracking or bad lots released, both discovered at customer-return time

iteration_protocol.trigger: a new base metal, underlayer, finish or plating-bath change is introduced
iteration_protocol.action: requalify with three conforming lots and re-run the full acceptance battery, then re-map the grade gates

iteration_protocol.trigger: a value-engineering cost-down lever is proposed
iteration_protocol.action: hold the gate, move the one lever toward the knee, re-run the same battery, and accept only if every gate re-passes

iteration_protocol.trigger: field returns show wear-through, tarnish or green skin staining
iteration_protocol.action: tighten the thickness/barrier at the failing point and re-grade, checking for a crossed gate

iteration_protocol.trigger: a regulation changes (REACH nickel limit, FTC guides, a market's marking law)
iteration_protocol.action: re-check the nickel and label/thickness gates and the claims mapped to them

iteration_protocol.trigger: the gold or rhodium price moves materially
iteration_protocol.action: re-derive the cost drivers and re-locate the knee on the cost-quality curve, re-checking which levers now pay
re-evaluate batch economics and the in-house-vs-send-out balance while keeping the per-batch floor

iteration_protocol.trigger: a live accredited test result or a known forward metal price lands
iteration_protocol.action: harden the corresponding estimate, update the honesty ledger, and re-issue the hand-off spec

priority_rationale: The quality-grade definition, the five/six test gates and the thickness ladder come first because every downstream judgement depends on a gate-based, worst-case-point definition of quality and on the citeable tests that measure it; the acceptance plan and grade-gate map next, because they assemble those tests into what gates the high-quality claim; the cost drivers and the cost-quality curve then convert quality into a spend tradeoff with a floor and a knee; the five value-engineering levers, the perceived-vs-real split and the false-economy catalogue apply the curve to concrete cost-downs; and the decision protocol, honesty ledger and hand-off come last because they enforce the hold-gate/move-one-lever/re-test loop and compose the graded, cost-engineered spec with its binding conditions before the pricing and assortment specialists take over.
